sugestoes.texto: `parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns a SafeParseReturnType, so the credential key is saved as `{success, data}`. On the next request, `googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key)` fails for every Google Calendar user whose token was refreshed. Store `.data`, and check `.success` first.

`prisma` is used here but never imported in this file, so `getClient` throws a ReferenceError and every Salesforce operation fails. The connection is also built from the old `credentialKey.access_token` instead of the new token, and the network refresh plus DB write runs every time the service is constructed.

The credential ID is passed to `refreshOAuthTokens` where a user ID is expected, so the sync endpoint receives the wrong `calcomUserId` and may return another user's tokens. Pass the credential's `userId`.

In sync mode this returns a raw fetch `Response`. Google expects `res.data` (gaxios), HubSpot expects a token object, and the Zoho services expect `axios.data`, so all of them crash or store `undefined` tokens when credential syncing is enabled. Normalize the result per caller, or return parsed JSON and adapt each caller to it.

`z.string().toString()` returns "[object Object]", so both computed keys collapse into one literal key and the schema does not validate any expiry. Because extra keys are stripped, the parsed data also drops the expiry and other token fields that callers depend on. Use `z.object({ access_token: z.string() }).passthrough()` instead.

`parseRefreshTokenResponse` throws on an invalid response, so the old fallback that logged the MS error and kept the existing credentials is gone. The `tokenResponse.success &&` check on the next line is now dead code, and the error now reaches callers as an exception, without the MS response detail that used to be logged.

The webhook secret is compared with `!==`, which is not constant-time, so an attacker can learn the secret through timing differences. Anyone who recovers it can overwrite any user's app credentials. Compare with `crypto.timingSafeEqual`, and reject header values that are arrays or missing.

If two webhook calls for the same `userId`/`appSlug` arrive at once, both can pass `findFirst` before either inserts, so both `create` calls succeed and the user ends up with two credential rows. Later lookups then pick one of them arbitrarily. Run the lookup and the write inside a serialized `prisma.$transaction`, or add a unique constraint on (userId, appId) and use `upsert`.

Every Salesforce service instantiation now makes a blocking call to the Salesforce OAuth endpoint and does a `prisma.credential.update`, even when the stored access token is still valid. That adds latency to every CRM event and puts unnecessary load on Salesforce's token endpoint, where rate limits apply. Refresh only when the token has expired, or when jsforce reports an invalid session through its `refresh` event.

issues.descricao: The new app-credential webhook checks its shared secret with a plain !== string comparison instead of a constant-time comparison, leaking timing information about the secret.

comentarios.texto: Direct !== comparison of webhook secret leaks via timing attack. Use constant-time comparison (e.g., crypto.timingSafeEqual on hashed/buffered values with length check) instead of `req.headers[...] !== process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`.

The webhook authenticates a secret using direct string inequality, which is not constant-time and can leak information about the secret through comparison timing. Compare fixed-length representations using a constant-time primitive (such as crypto.timingSafeEqual), handling absent or malformed headers safely, instead of comparing the secret strings directly.

The webhook secret is compared with the `!==` operator, which short-circuits on the first differing byte and leaks the secret via response timing (timing attack). An attacker can iteratively recover CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET and then forge requests that create/update arbitrary user credential keys (decrypted with the AES key) via this endpoint. Use a constant-time comparison, e.g. crypto.timingSafeEqual on equal-length buffers, guarding for length mismatch first.

issues.descricao: The webhook parses the body with zod .parse and decrypts/JSON-parses the keys without error handling, so invalid payloads produce 500 errors instead of 400 responses.
issues.textoGolden: The `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse` function can throw on invalid payloads, resulting in 500 Internal Server Errors instead of the expected 400 Bad Request responses. This can lead to confusion for clients and hinder proper error handling.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: zod parse, symmetricDecrypt and JSON.parse throw unhandled (no try/catch) with no method guard. WHY: Invalid body/keys or GET request crashes handler with 500 and leaks stack, instead of 400/405. HOW: Wrap parse/decrypt in try/catch returning 400 and restrict to POST.

schema .parse plus symmetricDecrypt/JSON.parse throw unhandled (ZodError, decrypt error, SyntaxError) on invalid body or tampered keys, crashing webhook with 500. Use safeParse and try/catch with 400 responses.

issues.descricao: The webhook's non-atomic findFirst-then-create lets concurrent deliveries for the same user and app insert duplicate credential rows.

comentarios.texto: The webhook performs a non-atomic findFirst followed by create when no credential exists. Concurrent deliveries for the same user and app can both observe no row and insert duplicates because Credential has no unique userId/appId constraint; subsequent findFirst updates only one duplicate, leaving competing credentials stale. Serialize the lookup/create operation for each user/app pair or introduce an appropriate uniqueness constraint and atomic upsert.

issues.descricao: parseRefreshTokenResponse writes the hardcoded string 'refresh_token' when the refresh response omits a refresh token, so the stored credential gets an invalid refresh token and later refreshes fail.
issues.textoGolden: The parseRefreshTokenResponse function incorrectly sets refresh_token to the hardcoded string 'refresh_token' when it's missing from the OAuth refresh token response. This invalidates the token, breaking subsequent token refreshes and causing authentication failures.

comentarios.texto: The parser fabricates the literal refresh token "refresh_token" whenever a successful response omits refresh_token, including when synchronization is disabled. Office365's response schema explicitly permits that omission, and its caller merges parsed data over existing credentials, replacing the valid saved refresh token with this invalid value and breaking the next refresh. Leave the property absent so the existing token survives the merge.

When a refresh response omits refresh_token, this helper manufactures the hardcoded credential "refresh_token". Callers such as Office365 merge this into stored credentials, overwriting the valid existing refresh token and causing subsequent provider refreshes to use a predictable invalid token. Leave the field absent and preserve the existing credential when omission is allowed by the provider, or reject the response when a refresh token is required; do not substitute a literal authentication token.

WHAT: Missing refresh_token is replaced with literal string "refresh_token". WHY: Stores bogus refresh token in DB, breaking all future refreshes and masking provider errors. HOW: Preserve existing credential refresh_token or throw instead of injecting placeholder.

issues.descricao: minimumTokenResponseSchema uses computed keys from z.string().toString(), which produce a literal key rather than a wildcard, so the sync-mode schema does not validate or keep expiry and other token fields as intended.
issues.textoGolden: The Zod schema in parseRefreshTokenResponse uses computed property keys [z.string().toString()] and [z.string().optional().toString()] in minimumTokenResponseSchema, which is invalid Zod syntax and will throw a runtime error.

comentarios.texto: `[z.string().toString()]` evaluates to a fixed string key such as "ZodString", so minimumTokenResponseSchema requires a literal numeric property with that name. Every synced token response fails validation and throws "Invalid refreshed tokens were returned". Use `z.object({access_token: z.string()}).passthrough()` instead.

The computed keys `[z.string().toString()]` evaluate to the literal string "[object Object]", not a wildcard. The schema therefore requires a numeric property named "[object Object]", so safeParse always fails in credential-sync mode and the function throws "Invalid refreshed tokens were returned". Use `.passthrough()` on an object with access_token and optional numeric expiry fields instead.

The computed keys `[z.string().toString()]` evaluate to a literal string like "ZodString" and not to a wildcard. The schema therefore requires a numeric property with that nonsense name and never matches real token responses. In sync mode every refresh throws "Invalid refreshed tokens were returned". Use `.passthrough()` and a real expiry check instead.

issues.descricao: In sync mode refreshOAuthTokens returns a raw fetch Response, but callers expect their provider-specific shapes (res.data, axios .data, HubspotToken), so token refresh breaks for Google, Zoho and HubSpot when credential sharing is on.
issues.textoGolden: When APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are set, the refreshFunction helper returns the fetch Response, but several callers (for example GoogleCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting res.data, and HubspotCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting a HubspotToken) assume it returns the integration-specific token object. That mismatch will cause runtime errors in the sync-enabled path unless the return type or those call sites are adjusted.

comentarios.texto:
WHAT: In the credential-sharing branch `refreshOAuthTokens` returns the raw `fetch` `Response` object instead of a parsed token payload, yet several callers treat the result as an already-parsed token object.
WHY: Callers such as hubspot (`hubspotRefreshToken.expiresIn`), zoho-bigin (`tokenInfo.data.error`), zohocrm (`zohoCrmTokenInfo.data.error`) and googlecalendar (`res?.data`) read `.data`/token fields off the return value; a `Response` has neither, so the sync path yields `undefined`/`NaN` or throws a TypeError — the feature's primary code path is broken for those apps.
HOW: Parse the response (e.g. `const data = await response.json(); return data;`) before returning, or make every caller await the appropriate response handler.

In sharing mode refreshOAuthTokens returns the raw fetch Response (no `.data`), but the google caller reads `res?.data` and then `token.access_token`, throwing a TypeError swallowed by the catch, so the token is never refreshed.

`res?.data` assumes the value returned by refreshOAuthTokens has a `.data` field (true for the `fetchTokens.res` branch), but when APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED the helper returns a raw `fetch()` Response, which has no `.data`. Then `token.access_token` throws. Either parse the shared-mode Response here or have refreshOAuthTokens return a normalized `{ data }` shape.

issues.descricao: Google Calendar persists the safeParse result object instead of its data as the credential key, corrupting the stored credential so later reads fail.
issues.textoGolden: parseRefreshTokenResponse returns a Zod safeParse result ({ success, data, error }), not the credential key object. Persisting that as key stores the wrapper instead of the token payload; we should store the parsed data or use schema parse.

comentarios.texto: parseRefreshTokenResponse returns a SafeParse result {success,data}, not the parsed key. Storing it directly as `key` writes the wrapper to the credential. Unwrap like other callers: check .success and use .data.

parseRefreshTokenResponse returns SafeParse result {success,data}, but call site stores that wrapper as credential `key` (previously googleCredentialSchema.parse() returned the plain object). Store `key.data` / handle wrapper, otherwise persisted credential becomes {success,data} shape and subsequent credential reads fail.

parseRefreshTokenResponse returns SafeParse wrapper {success,data} but code stores the whole wrapper as credential.key. Office365calendar in same PR unwraps via .data. Persisted credential will be {success,data} instead of tokens, so next load fails validation. Unwrap to .data after success check.

issues.descricao: After switching to parseRefreshTokenResponse, the tokenResponse.success check in Office365 refreshAccessToken is dead code and the previous error logging was dropped.

comentarios.texto: parseRefreshTokenResponse now throws when parsing fails, so the `tokenResponse.success` check on the next line is dead code and the previous error logging was removed. A failed refresh now throws out of refreshAccessToken instead of keeping the old credentials. Catch the error or restore the previous handling.

issues.descricao: Salesforce getClient now refreshes the OAuth token and writes the credential on every service construction, adding a network round trip and DB write even when the access token is valid.

comentarios.texto: getClient now unconditionally exchanges the Salesforce refresh token on every service construction, even when the saved access token is valid. Each constructor invocation adds a blocking OAuth network round trip and credential database write before any Salesforce operation, replacing jsforce's existing on-demand refresh behavior. Keep refresh on demand or guard the exchange with a token-expiration check.

issues.textoGolden: The `refreshOAuthTokens` function is passed `credentialId` instead of `userId`, which breaks the credential sync functionality by causing incorrect user lookups. This issue can lead to failures in syncing user credentials, impacting user experience.

comentarios.texto:
WHAT: The 3rd argument to `refreshOAuthTokens` is `credentialId` (= `credential.id`, line 53), but the function's parameter is `userId` (`refreshOAuthTokens(refreshFunction, appSlug, userId)`).
WHY: When APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED, the sync endpoint is sent `calcomUserId: <credential id>` instead of the user id, so Bigin credentials are synced against the wrong/non-existent user (all other apps correctly pass `credential.userId`).
HOW: Pass `credential.userId` instead of `credentialId` as the third argument.

refreshOAuthTokens' third parameter is the Cal.com userId (used as `calcomUserId` in the sync request and to decide whether sharing runs), but this call passes `credentialId`. Every other caller passes `credential.userId`, so the credential-sync endpoint receives a credential row id as the user id and shared credentials are fetched/updated for the wrong identity. Pass `credential.userId` here.

refreshOAuthTokens' third parameter is `userId` (declared in refreshOAuthTokens.ts line 3 and used as `calcomUserId: userId.toString()`), but this call passes `credentialId` (the Credential row id, line 53) instead of the user id. When credential sharing is enabled the customer's sync endpoint receives a credential id labelled as calcomUserId and cannot resolve the correct Cal.com user. Pass `credential.userId` (the BiginToken/credential payload carries it) or plumb the user id through refreshAccessToken.

issues.descricao: Salesforce checks response.statusText !== 'OK' instead of response.ok when refreshing the token, which can misclassify successful responses, and then ignores the refreshed token.
issues.textoGolden: The Salesforce integration checks `response.statusText` instead of `response.ok` when handling OAuth token refresh responses. This can lead to unreliable behavior, as a successful response may not be correctly identified, resulting in the use of stale credentials and potential authentication failures.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: Checks response.statusText !== "OK" instead of response.ok and builds jsforce.Connection from stale credentialKey.access_token/instance_url ignoring accessTokenParsed.data. WHY: Refresh never takes effect (old token reused) and valid refreshes can throw on runtimes where statusText is empty. HOW: Check !response.ok and use parsed access_token/instance_url for connection and DB update.

issues.textoGolden: The `jsforce.Connection` is created using stale `credentialKey.access_token` and `credentialKey.instance_url` after a token refresh, which can lead to authentication failures and incorrect data access. Ensure that the connection is established using the refreshed token values instead.

comentarios.texto:
WHAT: The new block fetches and persists a fresh access token (`accessTokenParsed.data`) but then creates the `jsforce.Connection` with the stale `credentialKey.access_token` (line 106) instead of the just-refreshed token.
WHY: The refreshed token is written to the DB but never used for the connection; if the old token was expired, jsforce must refresh again (extra round trip) or fail, and the DB/connection state diverge.
HOW: Pass the new access token (`accessTokenParsed.data.access_token`) to the `jsforce.Connection`.

issues.descricao: The diff-trimming code computes common prefix and suffix independently, so they can overlap and substring throws StringIndexOutOfBoundsException, crashing the verifier instead of reporting the illegal HTML.

comentarios.texto: The common prefix (start) and common suffix (end) are computed independently and can overlap, for example value "aa" vs sanitized "a". Then substring(start, length - end) gets begin > end and throws StringIndexOutOfBoundsException, so the verifier crashes instead of reporting the illegal HTML. Bound the suffix scan so that start + end <= min(value.length(), sanitized.length()), e.g. `while (end < min - start && ...)`.

The common prefix and common suffix are computed independently and can overlap, so `sanitized.substring(start, sanitized.length() - end)` can have start > end and throw StringIndexOutOfBoundsException. This crashes the verifier instead of reporting 'Illegal HTML'. Cap the suffix scan with `end < Math.min(value.length(), sanitized.length()) - start`.

WHY: Throws StringIndexOutOfBoundsException inside the key loop and crashes verification instead of reporting Illegal HTML. HOW: Clamp end so start+end <= min lengths, e.g. stop suffix scan when end >= length-start.

issues.descricao: The account and admin UI bundles now use Java MessageFormat placeholders and choice syntax for error-invalid-multivalued-size, but i18next expects {{n}}, so the UI shows literal {0}/{1}/{2} and the raw choice text.

comentarios.texto: The admin-ui bundle is consumed by react-i18next, which interpolates with double-brace `{{0}}` syntax (the previous value was `Attribute {{0}} ... {{2}}`). This line was rewritten to Java MessageFormat/ICU syntax (`{0}` ... `{2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}`), which i18next does not understand: the placeholders will not be substituted and the literal `{2,choice,...}` text will be shown to users. Keep the JS-side value in `{{0}}` form (and don't introduce ICU ChoiceFormat into the JS bundle); the ICU/choice spelling belongs only in the Java theme properties.

Restore `{{0}}`-style placeholders for the JS bundle.

The account-ui bundle is consumed by i18next, which interpolates with double braces (the original string was `Attribute {{0}} must have at least {{1}} and at most {{2}} value(s).`). sugestoes.texto: When user_count is an exact multiple of limit (for example 50 members with limit 50), totalPages is one too high, so the UI shows '1/2' and Next stays enabled. Clicking Next sets offset to user_count and loads an empty page. Compute it with Math.ceil(user_count / limit).

`group.users.delete(user_id)` removes the join row directly. It skips the cleanup that the old `usernames=`/`destroy_deletions` path did: GroupUser destroy callbacks and resetting `users.primary_group_id`. A removed member who had this group as their primary group keeps that primary_group_id and still shows its flair/title. Look up the user and call `group.remove(user)`, and clear primary_group_id when it matches this group.

findMembers now asks for one page (limit 50, offset 0), and the public members.hbs has no next/previous controls. Members after the 50th can no longer be seen on the group page, whereas before every member of a non-automatic group was listed. Add pagination to the public members page or load the remaining pages.

`Group#add` runs `users.push(user)` on an already-saved group, which inserts the row right away. Because `group_users` has a UNIQUE (group_id, user_id) index, entering a username that is already a member raises `ActiveRecord::RecordNotUnique`. The request then fails with a 500, and earlier usernames in the same batch may already have been added. Skip users who are already members, or rescue the duplicate, before calling `group.add`.

issues.descricao: The admin group pager computes total pages as floor(user_count / limit) + 1, so when the member count is an exact multiple of the limit it shows an extra page and Next navigates to an empty member list.
issues.textoGolden: The `totalPages` calculation using `Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1` produces an extra page when `user_count` is an exact multiple of `limit`, leading to incorrect pagination. For example, with 100 users and a limit of 50, it reports 3 pages instead of 2, allowing navigation to an empty page.

comentarios.texto: totalPages (and currentPage) use `Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1`, which is an off-by-one when user_count is an exact multiple of limit (e.g. 50 members, limit 50 → reports 2 pages although only 1 exists). This leaves `showingLast` false on the real last page, so 'next' navigates to an empty page at offset=user_count. Use `Math.ceil(user_count / limit)` (and compute currentPage consistently) to get the correct page count.

totalPages is off by one when user_count is an exact multiple of limit: `Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1` gives 2 for user_count=50, limit=50, although 50 members occupy exactly one page. Correct it to `Math.ceil(this.get('user_count') / this.get('limit'))`. Effect: for a group whose member count is a multiple of the page size, totalPages is one too high, showingLast remains false so the 'next' link stays enabled, and clicking it navigates to a phantom empty page.

`totalPages` uses `Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1`, which over-counts by one whenever `user_count` is an exact multiple of `limit` (e.g. 50 members with limit 50 yields 2 pages instead of 1). Since `showingLast` is `propertyEqual("currentPage", "totalPages")`, on a full last page `showingLast` is false, so the `next` action stays enabled and advances `offset` to `user_count`, rendering an empty page labeled as the last page. Use `Math.ceil(user_count / limit)` (with the zero-member guard) so the count matches the real number of pages.

issues.descricao: Several Group model functions (findMembers, destroy, userCountDisplay) return a value on some paths and undefined on others, triggering consistent-return lint warnings.
issues.textoGolden: Expected to return a value at the end of function - code paths without explicit returns will return undefined

issues.descricao: Paging actions fire overlapping member requests and each response unconditionally overwrites offset and members, so a stale response arriving last can revert the list to an earlier page.

comentarios.texto: Guard against stale member-fetch responses before updating the model. `next` updates offset immediately and leaves navigation enabled, so with at least three pages two rapid clicks issue requests for offsets 50 and 100. If the offset-100 response arrives first and the offset-50 response arrives last, this unconditional `setProperties` resets both offset and members to the older page, undoing the latest navigation. Refreshes after membership changes can similarly be overwritten by an earlier fetch. Track a per-model request generation and apply only the latest response, or serialize navigation and refresh requests.

issues.descricao: The public members endpoint now always caps results at 50 per page, but the public group members page has no pagination, so groups with more than 50 members are silently truncated for users.

comentarios.texto: The public members route now loads only the model's default 50-member page without providing any way to request subsequent pages. The public group/members.hbs template only renders members and has no Next/Previous controls, so members after the first 50 become inaccessible (manual groups previously returned all members). Add public pagination controls and actions that update offset and reload members.

The new default limit applies to nonautomatic groups as well, but the public group-members route still calls findMembers() only once and its template simply iterates members without pagination. Previously this endpoint returned every member of a nonautomatic group; now a group with more than 50 members exposes only the first 50 on its public members page, with no way to reach the rest. Update that consumer to fetch subsequent pages or provide pagination when introducing this endpoint contract.

Provide pagination or load subsequent pages for the public group-members view. findMembers now requests only 50 members, and this route calls it only once while its template simply iterates members without navigation. Custom groups previously returned all members, so groups larger than 50 now have members that cannot be viewed on this page.

issues.descricao: Creating a group ignores the alias_level the admin selected, saving only name and visibility, so new groups keep the default alias level.

comentarios.texto: Persist params[:alias_level] when creating a group, just as update does. The creation form exposes aliasLevelOptions and group.asJSON sends the selected alias_level, but create saves only name and visible. A newly created group therefore retains the default alias level instead of the administrator's selection.

issues.descricao: Removing a member deletes the membership row directly and skips clearing the user's primary_group_id, so a removed user can keep this group as their primary group.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: remove_member uses group.users.delete(user_id) instead of the Group#remove destroy path. WHY: bypasses GroupUser destroy callbacks and primary_group_id cleanup done in destroy_deletions, leaving stale membership side-effects (e.g. dangling primary_group_id). HOW: load the User and call group.remove(user).

Removing a member with group.users.delete bypasses the primary_group_id cleanup previously performed by Group#destroy_deletions during usernames updates. A user whose primary group is this group remains associated with it as their primary group after membership removal, leaving stale primary-group state used by user administration and post serialization. Clear primary_group_id for the removed user when it equals this group's id as part of the removal operation.

issues.descricao: The remove_member spec issues a PUT request although the route only maps DELETE to remove_member, so the test uses a verb never routed in production.
issues.textoGolden: The remove_member test uses xhr :put to call the remove_member action, but the route defines delete 'members' => 'groups#remove_member' requiring DELETE method.

comentarios.texto: This example sends `xhr :put, :remove_member`, but the PR maps `remove_member` only to DELETE (`delete "members" => "groups#remove_member"`); PUT on that path routes to `groups#add_members`. Controller specs bypass the router, so the example still lands on `remove_member` and passes regardless — it would still pass if the DELETE route were missing or wired to the wrong action, leaving the newly introduced verb/action pairing untested. Use `xhr :delete, :remove_member`, as the sibling example at line 125 already does.

The test 'cannot remove members from automatic groups' sends `xhr :put, :remove_member`, but the route is `delete "members" => "groups#remove_member"`. It exercises the action with a verb that is never routed in production. Use `xhr :delete, :remove_member, group_id: 1, user_id: 42` so the test matches the real request.

issues.descricao: Admin add_members pushes every username into group.users without skipping existing members, so adding someone already in the group hits the unique group_users index, returns a 500 and leaves earlier users partially added.
The public group members endpoint takes `limit` from params with no upper bound or positivity check, letting a visitor request huge pages or trigger a 500 with a negative limit.
Admin remove_member calls group.users.delete with a raw integer id, which raises RecordNotFound (404/500) when the user is not or no longer a member, e.g. on concurrent removal.
Admin remove_member deletes memberships with group.users.delete, which skips GroupUser callbacks, so the cached groups.user_count is never decremented and stays inflated.
Group member pagination is off by one when user_count is a multiple of limit: Next moves to offset == user_count and shows an empty page.
`add_members` runs one User query per username; load all users with a single `User.where(username: ...)` query.

sugestoes.texto: Ruby has no method overloading, so this second `downsize` definition replaces the 5-argument `downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts)`. As a result, `Jobs::ResizeEmoji` (`OptimizedImage.downsize(path, path, 100, 100, opts)`) now raises ArgumentError. Use a distinct name for the dimension-string variant, or keep one method that accepts either form.

For animated GIFs, `downsize` routes to `gifsicle --resize-fit 80%`, which takes WxH and likely rejects a percentage. The loop never checks the boolean result, so it burns 5 failed attempts and keeps the oversized file. Stop the loop when `downsize` returns false, and avoid passing a percentage geometry to the gifsicle path.

In the API URL path, the tempfile path includes the request's `type` param (`"discourse-upload-#{type}"` from FileHelper.download), and this new call passes that path into `convert_with`, which runs it unquoted in a backtick shell command. A `type` value such as `x$(cmd)` gives command execution to any API key holder. Validate `type` against an allowlist, or escape arguments with `Shellwords.escape` in `convert_with`.

issues.descricao: downsize is defined twice in OptimizedImage; the new (from, to, dimensions, opts) version overrides the (max_width, max_height) one, so existing callers such as ResizeEmoji that pass width and height now raise ArgumentError.
issues.textoGolden: The downsize method is defined twice. The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: A second `def self.downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={})` is defined that overrides the existing `downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})` at lines 145-147. WHY: Ruby uses the last definition, so the effective downsize now only accepts 3-4 args, and the existing caller app/jobs/regular/resize_emoji.rb:14 (`OptimizedImage.downsize(path, path, 100, 100, opts)`) passes 5 args and raises ArgumentError (wrong number of arguments, given 5, expected 3..4), breaking emoji resizing. HOW: Remove the duplicate; keep a single downsize method whose signature matches all callers (the 4-arg uploads_controller call `downsize(path, path, "80%", allow_animation: ...)` and the 5-arg ResizeEmoji call), or rename one of them.

`downsize` is defined twice: the original 5-param form `downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts)` at lines 145-147 and the new 4-param form `downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts)` at lines 149-151. Ruby keeps only the last definition, so the effective signature is now 4 params and the 5-param version is dead code. The pre-existing consumer app/jobs/regular/resize_emoji.rb:14 still calls `OptimizedImage.downsize(path, path, 100, 100, opts)` with 5 positional args, which now raises ArgumentError on every emoji resize. Either update that caller to the new `dimensions` form or remove the redundant override so the old signature keeps working.

`self.downsize` is defined twice in the same class scope (line 145 `(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})` and the new line 149 `(from, to, dimensions, opts={})`). Ruby keeps only the last definition, so the 4-argument version is dead and unreachable. The existing caller `OptimizedImage.downsize(path, path, 100, 100, opts)` in app/jobs/regular/resize_emoji.rb:14 passes 5 arguments and will now raise ArgumentError (expected 3..4). Remove the duplicate definition (keep only the `dimensions`-based one, or convert resize_emoji's call), otherwise emoji resizing breaks.

issues.descricao: The client-side upload size check hardcodes 10 MB instead of the per-type max_<type>_size_kb setting, so attachment limits diverge from the server: larger allowed attachments are blocked and smaller limits are only enforced server-side.
issues.textoGolden: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).

comentarios.texto: Hardcoded max size literal 10 * 1024 replaces site-setting-derived max size. Behavioral concern outside assigned class.

The fixed 10 MB client limit is applied to attachments as well as images, replacing max_attachment_size_kb. Sites configured to allow attachments larger than 10 MB can no longer upload those valid files through the composer, although UploadValidator still permits them. Apply the new input ceiling only to images and retain the configured attachment limit.

WHAT: Client check hardcodes maxSizeKB to 10*1024 instead of Discourse.SiteSettings['max_'+type+'_size_kb'], losing image vs attachment distinction. WHY: Sites with smaller max_attachment_size_kb pass client validation then fail server-side, and sites with limits >10MB incorrectly block valid uploads with wrong max_size_kb message. HOW: Restore per-type SiteSetting lookup (keep 10MB only as image downsize ceiling).

issues.descricao: The upload downsizing passes a percentage ('80%') as dimensions, but for animated GIFs the gifsicle path uses --resize-fit, which expects WxH geometry, so downsizing silently fails.
issues.textoGolden: Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.

comentarios.texto: The controller passes the percentage string `"80%"` as the dimensions argument to `OptimizedImage.downsize`, but the consumer requires explicit `WxH` geometry: the code this PR deleted built exactly `"#{width}x#{height}"`, and the animated path runs `gifsicle --resize-fit #{dimensions}`, which rejects a percentage. Pass an explicit size (e.g. a computed `"WxH"` from the max KB target) so the auto-downsize actually reduces the file, rather than silently no-oping and leaving oversized uploads.

Caller passes "80%" as dimensions to OptimizedImage.downsize, but the downsize/optimize instruction builders in optimized_image.rb expect explicit "WxH" geometry (interpolated as -resize #{dimensions}\>). A bare percentage does not satisfy that contract and will produce a malformed geometry. Fix the caller to supply WxH dimensions or add explicit percentage handling to the callee.

issues.descricao: Auto-downsizing passes the upload tempfile path, which lacks a .gif extension, so the animated branch is never chosen and convert keeps only the first frame, flattening oversized animated GIFs.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: The new auto-downsize call passes a tempfile path whose name has no `.GIF` extension, so `optimize` never selects the animated branch (`method_name += "_animated" if opts[:allow_animation] && from =~ /\.GIF$/i`) and uses `downsize_instructions`, which runs `convert from[0]` and keeps only the first frame. WHY: Animated GIFs larger than max_image_size_kb that are uploaded through this path have their animation flattened to a single frame even though SiteSetting.allow_animated_thumbnails is enabled. HOW: Detect the image type from the original filename/content-type rather than the tempfile path (or pass a flag) so the gifsicle animated downsize path is used for GIF inputs.

Passing the multipart tempfile path to downsize prevents animation detection when that path does not end in .gif, even when allow_animated_thumbnails is enabled. OptimizedImage.optimize checks the path suffix and otherwise uses convert with input[0], so oversized animated GIF uploads are permanently flattened to their first frame. Preserve the original image extension in the processing path or pass the image format explicitly to select animated processing.

issues.descricao: The comment promises images are reduced to the allowed size, but the loop only tries five 80% reductions with no guarantee of reaching the limit.

comentarios.texto: The comment says large images are "automatically reduced to allowed size", but the loop only resizes by 80% up to 5 attempts (≈0.33× of the original in the best case) and then stops without any check that the result actually meets `max_image_size_kb`. The prose promises a guarantee the code does not provide; either make the loop actually converge to the allowed size or reword the comment to state that the image is only attempted to be reduced.

issues.descricao: The downsize retry loop ignores the false return of a failed conversion and repeats the same failing ImageMagick call up to five times.

comentarios.texto: The retry loop ignores downsize's false return value and retries failed conversions while the file remains oversized. convert_with returns false on converter failure, so an unsupported or malformed oversized image launches the same failing external conversion up to five times per upload without any changed input. Break on a failed downsize result and return an upload error rather than repeating the conversion.

WHAT: Downsize loop ignores OptimizedImage.downsize return value and retries up to 5 times unconditionally while checking tempfile.size. WHY: Failed converts (e.g. SVG, invalid 80%> geometry, corrupt image) burn 5 ImageMagick runs then Upload.create_for still runs with oversized/unmodified file and fails validation, wasting CPU and breaking the feature. HOW: Break on false return and handle failure.

issues.descricao: Claims up to five synchronous ImageMagick runs per oversized upload block request threads and enable DoS.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: Up to 5 synchronous OptimizedImage.downsize + ImageOptim convert runs execute inline in create_upload request cycle for every oversized image. WHY: Blocks the Rails request thread with CPU-intensive shell-outs per upload, enabling easy request-thread exhaustion/DoS with large images. HOW: Move downsizing to background job or enforce single-pass/timeout.

issues.descricao: Claims the downsize loop checking tempfile.size may never terminate because of a stale cached size, causing infinite loops.
issues.textoGolden: The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.

issues.descricao: The 413 upload error message states a hard-coded 10 MB maximum that may not match the limit the server or web server actually enforces.

The upload tempfile path, which for API URL uploads embeds the request-controlled type param, is now passed to OptimizedImage.downsize and run unescaped in a shell via backticks, allowing command injection through type.
Oversized SVG uploads go through the new ImageMagick downsize loop because SVG counts as an image, so the vector file is rasterized or corrupted in place before Upload.create_for parses it as SVG.

sugestoes.texto: Processes created with `get_context("spawn").Process` are `SpawnProcess` instances, which do not subclass `multiprocessing.Process`. The isinstance check is therefore always false and `kill()` never runs. A process restarted for `hang` keeps running next to its replacement, so two flushers drain the same shards and produce duplicate segments. Use `multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess` as the isinstance target, or check `not isinstance(process, threading.Thread)`, as the old unconditional `kill()` effectively did.

Once the deadline passes, `break` leaves the loop, so the remaining processes are neither waited on nor terminated and can outlive shutdown or a rebalance. The terminate guard also uses `multiprocessing.Process`, which never matches `SpawnProcess`. Keep iterating after the deadline so every process gets terminated, and check for `BaseProcess` instead.

`get_memory_info` calls `iter_cluster_memory_usage` on the same Redis cluster for every per-process buffer. Each submit therefore repeats the cluster-wide INFO scan N times and adds up identical numbers. Query the cluster once, for example through the first buffer or a dedicated buffer.

issues.descricao: The wait_produce timer is tagged with 'shards' while sibling flusher metrics use 'shard' for the same value, so per-shard dashboards miss it.
issues.textoGolden: In the SpanFlusher flush loop, metric tags inconsistently use 'shard' (e.g., in spans.buffer.flusher.produce and spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes) and 'shards' (in spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce) for the same shard identifier value. This prevents correct metric aggregation across flush stages — dashboards and alerts filtering by tag 'shard' will miss data tagged as 'shards' and vice versa.

comentarios.texto: The `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` timer is tagged with the key `"shards"`, while the other two metrics emitted in this same loop (`spans.buffer.flusher.produce` at line 185 and `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` at line 195) use the key `"shard"`. All three carry the same `shard_tag` value, so this is a pure key-name disagreement: any dashboard or alert that groups/filters by the `shard` tag will silently receive no data from `wait_produce`. Rename the tag key to `"shard"` so all flusher metrics share one tag.

The `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` timer is tagged with key `shards` while every sibling metric introduced/updated in the same method (`spans.buffer.flusher.produce`, `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes`) uses the singular key `shard`. Anything consuming this metric family by the `shard` tag (dashboards, alerts, tag-based aggregation) will silently receive no data for `wait_produce`, and per-shard breakdowns of produce latency will be incomplete. Change the tag to `tags={"shard": shard_tag}` so the tag contract matches the other flusher metrics.

The wait_produce timer tags with "shards", while the sibling metrics in the same loop use "shard" for the same value (shard_tag). Use one tag key, "shard", so queries and dashboards that group by it cover all of these metrics.

issues.descricao: The time.sleep(0.1) added to test_basic to let flusher threads process is a no-op because the test monkeypatches time.sleep.
issues.textoGolden: The test_basic function in test_consumer.py uses a monkeypatched time.sleep that returns immediately, but then calls time.sleep(0.1) expecting it to actually wait.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: The added synchronization point `time.sleep(0.1)` added after the second `step.poll()` is neutralized by the test's own `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)` at line 15 (same `time` module), so it does not actually wait. WHY: The comment says it 'Give[s] flusher threads time to process after drift change', but the call is a no-op, so the test still races the background flusher thread before `step.join()` and is liable to be flaky / to not exercise the intended post-drift flush path. HOW: Use a non-monkeypatched wait (e.g. capture the real sleep before patching, or use the flusher's thread/process join, or poll until `messages` is non-empty with a real timeout).

The added `time.sleep(0.1)` does not wait: line 15 of the same test does `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)`, which replaces `sleep` on the global `time` module, so this call (and the flusher's own `time.sleep`) is a no-op. The comment 'Give flusher threads time to process after drift change' is therefore false — the call returns instantly and provides no synchronisation, so the test does not actually wait for the flusher to process after the drift change. Either synchronise on a real condition (e.g. wait until the expected message is produced) or, if the original `time.sleep` is needed here, patch a module-scoped reference instead of the global `time.sleep`.

The added `time.sleep(0.1)` is a no-op because the test patches `time.sleep` to `lambda _: None`, so nothing waits for the flusher threads before `step.join()` and the `messages` assertion. Replace it with a condition-based wait, such as polling until `messages` is non-empty with a deadline. Use the real sleep saved before patching if a delay is needed.

issues.descricao: The restart path only kills a hung flusher if it is a multiprocessing.Process, but spawn-context workers are SpawnProcess, so hung processes are never killed and a duplicate flusher is started for the same shards.
issues.textoGolden: Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.

comentarios.texto: The new isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process) guard does not match the SpawnProcess instances created by self.mp_context.Process. When a worker hangs, the guard skips kill() and the replacement starts while the original worker remains alive, allowing overlapping flushing of the same shards if the original resumes and leaking hung workers. Check against multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess or self.mp_context.Process, and kill and join the old worker before replacing it.

The workers are created with get_context("spawn").Process, which produces SpawnProcess instances; these are not instances of multiprocessing.Process (the default-context Process class). Consequently this guard skips kill() for actual production workers. When a worker hangs, the replacement starts while the original remains alive and can resume flushing the same shards. Use multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess or the spawn-context Process class for the check, and fix the identical check in join() so shutdown also terminates surviving workers.

Workers created by multiprocessing.get_context("spawn").Process are SpawnProcess instances, not instances of the separate multiprocessing.Process class. Consequently this guard skips kill() for production workers. When a live worker exceeds max-unhealthy-seconds, the code starts a replacement and overwrites its handle while the original is still running. If the original resumes, both workers flush the same shards, and repeated hangs can exceed the configured process limit. Check against multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess (or explicitly distinguish threads) and stop the old worker before replacing it.

issues.descricao: join() breaks out of the per-process loop when the shared deadline expires, skipping termination of the remaining flusher processes and leaving them running after shutdown.
issues.textoGolden: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.

comentarios.texto: join() breaks out of the worker loop when the shared deadline expires, skipping cleanup for every remaining worker. If next_step.join consumes the timeout or an earlier worker exhausts it, remaining flushers can continue running after shutdown or partition reassignment. Use the deadline only to limit waiting and still terminate and reap every remaining process.

Do not break out of worker cleanup when the join deadline expires. If the first worker consumes the timeout, the next iteration breaks before terminating that worker or any subsequent workers. They may still be blocked in Redis or producer calls despite the shared stopped flag, leaving old workers running after strategy shutdown/reassignment. Apply the deadline only to waiting, and perform termination cleanup for every worker regardless of remaining time (using a type check that recognizes spawn-context workers).
join() waits for processes sequentially against a single shared deadline and breaks without terminating remaining processes once it expires, leaking them.

issues.descricao: The SpanFlusher docstring says it creates one process per shard, but shards are distributed across at most max_processes processes.

comentarios.texto: The docstring says the flusher "Creates one process per shard for parallel processing," but the code at lines 60-66 shares shards across a capped number of processes (num_processes = min(self.max_processes, len(buffer.assigned_shards)); each shard assigned via i % self.num_processes). With the new --flusher-processes default of 1, a single process handles every shard, so the documented contract is the opposite of the behaviour this PR introduces (confirmed by test_flusher_processes_limit, which asserts 4 shards served by 2 processes). Update the docstring to say shards are distributed across up to max_processes flusher processes.

The new docstring says this creates one process per shard, but workers are capped by max_processes and shards are distributed among them. In particular, the CLI default of 1 means all assigned shards share one process. Describe capped workers with potentially multiple shards per worker so callers do not rely on per-shard process isolation.

The docstring says the flusher 'Creates one process per shard', but the number of processes is capped by max_processes (--flusher-processes), and shards are shared across processes via i % num_processes. Reword it to say that shards are distributed across at most max_processes processes.

issues.descricao: max_processes uses a truthiness fallback, so --flusher-processes 0 silently becomes one process per shard instead of being rejected.

comentarios.texto: `max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` treats a falsy value as 'not provided'. The new `--flusher-processes` click option is `type=int`, so a user can pass `0`; that legitimate-but-falsy value is discarded and the flusher silently spawns one process per shard instead of honoring the requested limit. Use an explicit None check, e.g. `self.max_processes = max_processes if max_processes is not None else len(buffer.assigned_shards)` (and validate/reject 0 upstream).

An explicit max_processes=0 is treated as an omitted limit by `or`, so passing `--flusher-processes 0` starts one process per assigned shard instead of respecting or rejecting the supplied zero limit. The CLI accepts zero as an integer and the factory forwards it unchanged. Default only when max_processes is None, and explicitly validate that supplied process limits are positive so zero cannot silently enable potentially many workers.

`max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` uses a truthiness test, so an explicit 0 is treated as 'unset' and silently expands to one process per shard. Use `max_processes if max_processes is not None else len(buffer.assigned_shards)` and reject values below 1.

issues.descricao: A negative --flusher-processes value is not validated and makes SpanFlusher construction fail with KeyError.

comentarios.texto: `flusher_processes` is not validated to be >= 1. `self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` lets a negative value through (it is truthy), so `self.num_processes = min(self.max_processes, len(...))` becomes negative and `range(self.num_processes)` is empty, leaving `process_to_shards_map` as `{}`. The following loop computes `process_index = i % self.num_processes`, which for any negative divisor is 0, so `self.process_to_shards_map[0].append(shard)` raises KeyError and the consumer fails to construct. Since `flusher_processes` is exposed as an int CLI option (`--flusher-processes`), a negative value is reachable from configuration. Guard with `max(1, self.num_processes)` / validate the input.
negative max_processes flows through `or` guard into min() -> empty map -> KeyError on i % num_processes; empty assigned_shards yields zero processes.

issues.descricao: submit() queries cluster-wide Redis memory once per flusher buffer, repeating identical INFO calls per process on every submit.

comentarios.texto: The new loop calls get_memory_info() once per flusher buffer even though SpansBuffer.get_memory_info delegates to iter_cluster_memory_usage(self.client), which fetches INFO for the entire Redis cluster regardless of assigned_shards. With P flusher processes and memory backpressure enabled, each submitted batch now performs P identical cluster-wide memory queries on the consumer thread instead of one, increasing Redis traffic and blocking ingestion. Fetch cluster memory information once from a single buffer.
submit() loop calls buffer.get_memory_info() per flusher but each call is cluster-wide from same client, repeating identical INFO N× per submit.

issues.descricao: _create_process_for_shard is added but never called.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: `_create_process_for_shard(self, shard)` is newly added but has no caller anywhere (grep for `_create_process_for_shard(` finds only its definition); the restart path actually used is `_create_process_for_shards(process_index, shards)`. WHY: This is dead code that indicates the intended per-shard restart wiring was left incomplete — any future caller relying on restarting only the process owning a given shard will silently do nothing, and it is confusing which restart path is authoritative. HOW: Remove `_create_process_for_shard`, or wire it into `_ensure_processes_alive` if per-shard restart was intended.

issues.descricao: test_flusher_processes_limit counts assigned shards instead of checking that each shard is assigned exactly once.

comentarios.texto: The assertion counts shard entries rather than verifying shard assignment. A broken distribution such as {0: [0, 1], 1: [0, 1]} still passes all assertions in this test while shards 2 and 3 are never flushed. Assert that the flattened mapping contains exactly the expected assigned shards, with no duplicates (and verify each worker's shard buffer uses that mapping), rather than only asserting a total of four.

sugestoes.texto: `MetricAlertFire.detector_handler` points to this class, but it no longer implements `counter_names`, `get_dedupe_value`, `get_group_key_values` or the new abstract `build_occurrence_and_event_data`. As a result, `Detector.detector_handler` raises `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class` for every `metric_alert_fire` detector, where it used to return a working handler. Add stub implementations of the abstract members, or keep the old concrete `DetectorHandler` subclass until the stateful version is implemented.

sugestoes.texto: `twilio.scheduleSMS` returns undefined when SMS sending is locked, and it throws on a monthly rate-limit hit or a Twilio outage. These are temporary conditions, but each one now counts as a retry, so after two cron runs the reminder is permanently deleted even though its scheduledDate may be days away. Count retries only for permanent errors (e.g. invalid number), or leave the locked/rate-limited `undefined` case out of the retry count.

The `prisma.workflowReminder.update` inside the catch block has no error handling, so if it fails (e.g. the row was deleted concurrently with a P2025 error, or the DB call fails) the exception escapes the loop. All remaining reminders in that run are skipped and the cron returns an error. Wrap it in its own try/catch, or use `updateMany` with `{ increment: 1 }`, which does not throw on a missing row.

issues.descricao: retryCount is set to reminder.retryCount + 1 from a value read at the start of the run instead of an atomic increment, so overlapping runs can lose increments.
issues.textoGolden: Using retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 reads a possibly stale value and can lose increments under concurrency; consider an atomic increment via Prisma (increment: 1) to avoid race conditions (also applies to the similar update in the catch block).

comentarios.texto: WHAT: retryCount is incremented with a read-value computed at the start of the run (`retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1`) instead of an atomic increment. WHY: if two cron invocations overlap (or the same reminder is processed twice before the write commits), both read the same retryCount and both write N+1, so failures are undercounted and the reminder can loop forever without ever reaching the `retryCount > 1` deletion threshold. HOW: use `data: { retryCount: { increment: 1 } }` so the increment is atomic (the initial read value is then irrelevant).

`retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1` is a read-modify-write of the value fetched at the top of the handler, not an atomic increment. Two overlapping cron runs both read the same retryCount and both write the same +1, losing an update, so failed reminders can be retried indefinitely and never reach the `gt: 1` deletion threshold. Use Prisma's atomic `retryCount: { increment: 1 }` instead of computing from the stale in-memory value (same issue in the else branch at lines 179-186).

Retry counts are assigned from the stale findMany snapshot instead of incremented atomically, both here and in the catch branch. Two overlapping cron requests can each fail scheduling the same reminder with retryCount zero and both write one, so two failed attempts do not reach the deletion threshold and additional attempts are scheduled. Use Prisma's atomic retryCount increment operation in both failure branches.

Update the comment (or add the missing SMS filter to the retryCount branch) so the prose matches what the code actually deletes.

Because `retryCount` is a generic column on WorkflowReminder used by all reminder methods, this deleteMany now permanently deletes every reminder of ANY method (including EMAIL) whose retryCount exceeds 1, even though this cron is only supposed to clean up SMS reminders. Add `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` to this branch (or scope the whole where to SMS) so non-SMS reminders are never destroyed.

issues.descricao: The retry-count update inside the catch block is not guarded, so if it throws (for example the reminder was deleted concurrently) the error escapes the loop and the cron run fails, skipping the remaining reminders.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: the catch block performs an unguarded `prisma.workflowReminder.update` while handling the scheduling error. WHY: if this write itself rejects (e.g. the row was concurrently removed, or a transient DB error), the rejection is not caught and escapes the for-loop, aborting the whole cron run so all remaining reminders go unprocessed. HOW: wrap the retryCount update in its own try/catch (log and continue) so a failure to record the retry does not abort processing of the remaining reminders.

This new `prisma.workflowReminder.update` sits inside the catch block, which is NOT protected by any try/catch. If this update throws (e.g. the reminder was already removed by the `deleteMany` at the top of the file during a concurrent run -> Prisma P2025, or a transient DB error), the exception escapes the `for` loop and rejects the handler, so all remaining unscheduled reminders are skipped and the cron request fails. Previously the catch only did `console.log`, so a single bad reminder never aborted the batch and the endpoint always returned 200. Wrap this update in its own try/catch (or `updateMany`/catch-and-log) so a failed retry-count write cannot take down the whole scheduling run.

The new database update inside catch can itself throw when a reminder has been deleted during scheduling. Booking cancellation deletes reminders through handleCancelBooking and deleteScheduledSMSReminder, so a concurrent cancellation followed by a scheduling error now rejects the entire cron handler and prevents the remaining reminders from being processed. Use an updateMany filtered by the reminder ID to tolerate an already-deleted row, and guard errors from retry bookkeeping so they do not escape the per-reminder error handler.

WHY: Postgres cannot satisfy a two-way OR using the existing (method, scheduled, scheduledDate) index and will fall back to a sequential scan of the entire WorkflowReminder table on every cron invocation, turning a previously indexed delete into a full table scan as the table grows. HOW: add an index on retryCount (or restructure so each branch is index-usable), then re-check the query plan.

Unreachable branches in getBaseConditions: authConditions is always a truthy Prisma.Sql object (never null, NOTHING is `1=0`), so `else if (filterConditions)` and final `else { return NOTHING }` can never execute. WHAT: `getBaseConditions` returns `filterConditions` alone (no authorization predicate) when `authConditions` is falsy (`else if (filterConditions) { return filterConditions; }`). WHY: The WHERE clause returned to consumers then contains no ownership/authorization restriction, so a caller using it would return every booking matching the filters (e.g. all bookings for the given eventTypeId/memberUserId) regardless of the requesting user's org/team membership — an authorization-boundary bypass if `getAuthorizationConditions()` ever yields a falsy value. HOW: Always AND the authorization predicate with the filters and fall back to `NOTHING_CONDITION` when no auth predicate exists, e.g. `return filterConditions ? Prisma.sql`(${authConditions}) AND (${filterConditions})` : authConditions;` (or keep the `NOTHING_CONDITION` default when auth is missing).

The fixture creates a single booking that satisfies the auth condition (userId = user.id AND teamId IS NULL) and the filter condition (eventTypeId = eventType.id) independently, so getBaseConditions returning auth-only, filter-only, or the AND combination all yield the same single-row result asserted here. Only a `1=0` result would be caught. sugestoes.texto: When several requests hit an empty cache at once (startup, or after an error cached nil), each one waits for the write lock and then reads and decodes assets-manifest.json again, one after another, on hot paths like the index page and frontend settings. Check `entryPointAssetsCache` again after taking the write lock and return it if a concurrent caller already filled it (outside Dev mode).

issues.descricao: GetWebAssets does not re-check the cache after acquiring the write lock, so concurrent callers that missed the cache each reload the assets manifest.
issues.textoGolden: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: The exclusive lock acquired at line 48 is held (via defer on line 49) across the blocking file read / synchronous CDN HTTP request (lines 56-67) and there is no re-check of entryPointAssetsCache after acquiring the lock. WHY: On a cold cache, all concurrent callers (api/index.go:82, api/frontendsettings.go:62, middleware/recovery.go:141) block on the write lock and then each sequentially re-executes the full load (file I/O or blocking http.DefaultClient.Do), producing a thundering-herd serialization and N redundant loads instead of one; in Dev mode this happens on every request since the fast path is skipped, serializing all concurrent page loads. HOW: after `entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock()` re-check the cache (`if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil { return entryPointAssetsCache, nil }`) so only the first goroutine performs the load, and drop the defer in favor of releasing the lock immediately after assigning `entryPointAssetsCache = result` to avoid holding it during I/O.
cache is not re-checked under the lock after re-acquiring write Lock, so concurrent callers can each recompute web assets

The cache is not rechecked after acquiring the write lock, so concurrent production requests that initially observe a nil cache each reload and decode the manifest even after another request has populated it. During a cold-start request burst, these redundant filesystem reads and JSON decodes execute serially under the global lock, delaying queued page and frontend-settings requests and blocking cache readers while each reload runs. After acquiring the write lock, return the populated cache when cfg.Env != setting.Dev before performing asset loading.

issues.descricao: GetWebAssets holds a global exclusive mutex through the whole manifest load, so in Dev mode, where the cache is bypassed, every request serializes behind it.
